item.title: USDA, FBI breached by hackers amid spate of tech outages – reports
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Hackers breached the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the FBI, national media reported on Friday, amid deepening concerns over a spate of tech outages at key American institutions.

The breaches were first reported by NBC News and CNN respectively, and it remained unclear whether they were related and who was responsible.

Major outages in recent weeks have disrupted travel, communications and e-commerce for countless users across the US, even affecting a top-secret network at the National Security Agency.

Donald Trump has sought to calm the public, urging people to “relax”. Officials said the various outages were not linked to criminal activity.

The USDA told employees that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers was targeted in a cyber-attack, NBC reported on Friday, citing two former department officials.

The hackers may use the payments system as a back door to access more sensitive material, the former officials told NBC.

The USDA deals with “a bunch of scary biologic issues” and “if an adversary or a competitor were to have access to that same information … they could use our own research against us,” a former official was quoted as saying.

CNN said separately on Friday that the FBI was hacked for the second time since September.

The bureau was investigating an intrusion of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) by apparent hackers, CNN reported citing two people briefed on the probe.

The NCIC has a nationwide criminal information database linking federal, state and local law enforcement and is used to share information on warrants and background checks.

“Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety,” a former FBI official told CNN.

The former official expressed concerns that hackers “could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on”.

AFP has asked the FBI and the USDA for comment.

Ironically, the FBI director, Kash Patel, on Thursday appeared on the Fox News show hosted by Sean Hannity to tout measures his agency had implemented to thwart cyber-attacks.

Patel said the FBI and the US intelligence community would continue to “monitor those activities for nefarious actors” through an anti-cyber-attack initiative dubbed Operation Winter Shield.

“And when and if such an actor comes up, you can rest assured that this FBI is going to hunt them down,” Patel said.

The newly uncovered breaches at the FBI and the USDA were described as hacks, which are different from outages such as the ones that afflicted Microsoft Outlook and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) earlier in November.

In September, a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.

The Trump administration fired cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross on Thursday as criticism mounted over the string of major outages.

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-21 14:09 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/21/usda-fbi-outages-cyber-attack

item.title: Why Anthropic's blockbuster IPO couldn't escape the stock market correction
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

No one can say the Anthropic initial public offering wasn't a success for the company. Deal size and pricing were signs of what IPO experts say was insatiable demand for "ANT" shares. But what came within a day is something that investors better get used to: anxiety in the stock market about valuations being assigned to artificial intelligence revenue and business models that should keep Anthropic shares volatile in the period ahead.

The Anthropic IPO reinforces those fears rather than running counter to them, says Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital, which researches IPOs and manages the Renaissance IPO ETF (IPO).

"The volatility in the AI trade we've been seeing for the past few months stems from valuations and whether we are in a bubble, and that's been heightened and highlighted by the Anthropic IPO," Marquez said on "ETF Edge" on Friday.

And in the case of Anthropic, which finished trading Friday down 9%, the valuation anxiety becomes "so much more prevalent," she added, because it is a new stock.

It is not just any new stock, but one that has Wall Street adding downside risks to research notes likely never seen before, and which may be the greatest understatement (or most subtle equities research joke) in the history of earnings analysis. "Anthropic could develop AI systems which become fully autonomous and wipe out humanity which may lead to a serious decline in earnings," Seaport Research Partners analyst wrote Jay Goldberg wrote on Nov. 18.

"It was challenging company to value ... and it's very richly valued," Marquez said. "We're seeing something more reasonable and investors grappling now with where should this company actually be valued," she added.

The fact that Anthropic pulled off the deal in this market and was able to command the price it did was an achievement, according to Yuri Khodjamirian, chief investment officer at Tema ETFs, which offers multiple funds that invest in pre-IPO shares of companies and held Anthropic in its Tema Photonics & Optical ETF (LAZR) well before IPO day. "We have to remember they pulled off a very large IPO in the middle of a very severe market with the volatility in the tech sector specifically," Khodjamirian said on "ETF Edge."

"You always have to be a bit skeptical about 'oversubscribed' ... bankers put out all these numbers, but the reality is the IPO was successful and when you see the tech trade volatility ... welcome to the equities markets. This is what happens day-in and day-out," he said.

Khodjamirian says the investor demand for AI remains, but amid a reassessment of returns. And he says an equally hard task has now begun for Anthropic. Investors are unwinding positions in everything from tech stocks to gold and bitcoin, and repositioning for 2027 based on their new outlooks. "We are in a bit of vacuum," he said.

"From here on the market is trying trying to figure out what direction to go in," Khodjamirian said, whether that is based on Fed policy, geopolitics, the midterm elections results, or the AI trade. "In many cases, the chief investment officers I speak to, and the clients, say 'I'm just gonna take some risk off and wait and see until I get more info.' And with the Anthropic, the revenue picture and how the AI adoption curve progresses will be a vital stat to watch," he added.

Plenty of value has already been wiped out in tech, according to Khodjamirian, but investors need new signals to buy. That doesn't just go for Anthropic but for much of the market's tech leadership. "One of the things most difficult for investors to understand right now is some of the leadership in the market that has been taken by semiconductor companies," he said, adding that the peak was 22% of S&P 500 earnings. But these companies, like Nvidia and Micron, have a very different earnings profile from the rest of the market.

The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), which was down over 10% on Friday and around 15% for the week, was on pace for its worst week since September 2001, according to CNBC data on Friday afternoon. It also lost 15% in one week of March 2020. The tech sector of the S&P 500, tracked by the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK), turned in its worst weekly performance since the Covid crash.

Khodjamirian said while these stocks may look cheap on a P/E basis right now after the heavy selling, that requires faith in the earnings estimates, which he says will be more important as results are released for the next few years. "Right now it looks cheap, but will companies like Micron and Nvidia actually deliver?"

Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday, adding to its worst stretch of weekly performance since 2008. What's more, the single biggest trade in the options market on Friday was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF has a long way more to fall.

And the same caution about the outlook goes for Anthropic, he said. "That's why we need to watch Anthropic's annual recurring revenue number, because it is a key part of puzzle," he said.

Marquez said there is always hype in names like SpaceX and Anthropic when they go public, and it is hard to know whether the pricing of the deal is based on fundamentals, "but we just need more time and lots price discovery," she said. "It is not going to happen overnight," she added.

As an IPO researcher, she says this "discernment" is a healthy thing for the markets. There are few cases to look to as comps for Anthropic, other than SpaceX, and before that, way back to Facebook's IPO in 2012. And neither example is one of quick recovery. SpaceX shares remain well below their first-day closing price more than five months after its IPO. Facebook (now Meta), meanwhile, "did not do well for the first year after going public and we see where it is now. It's just the nature of these disruptive tech companies that come to market," Marquez said. "They lend themselves to more volatility and a longer period of price discovery for investors."…

Source: CNBC Top | Published: 2026-11-21 14:07 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/20/anthropic-ipo-ai-stock-market-selloff.html

item.title: Denmark to expel Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill US-Ukrainian rapper
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.

“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,” Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days.

“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he added.

Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.

Rasmussen also said that Denmark was considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians. “We have launched work at the European level to further tighten the rules governing access of Russian nationals to Europe,” he said. “We are now stepping up our efforts towards a halt to all non-essential visas.

“The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine. And we fully intend to continue supporting Ukraine.”

According to Reuters, Rasmussen sent a message on Friday evening to senior European diplomats proposing that the EU should halt tourist visas for Russian citizens and cease recognition of Russian non-biometric passports throughout the 29-nation Schengen free-travel zone.

“We must take concrete actions that project European strength and decisiveness,” the message said. “There is clear momentum to act decisively now, and we should seize this moment to replace our current patchwork of national measures with a truly unified EU-wide approach.”

The note also urged each EU member state to offer Russians more limited visas that do not allow travel to other countries in the Schengen zone, and to set tougher entry restrictions for serving and former Russian soldiers.

Police thwarted the alleged plot when they arrested three men with links to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Viktorovich Vasiliev, was due to perform at a concert on 25 September, which was then cancelled, officials said. Vasiliev holds US and Ukrainian nationality.

Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, the head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, said: “It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian intelligence services.”

According to prosecutors, the suspects were driving towards the concert venue north of Copenhagen with two loaded pistols and two knives when police arrested them at about 9.55pm, five minutes before the concert was due to begin. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening, police said.

One of the suspects had bought a ticket to the concert, according to the charges.

The suspects are charged under Section 108 of Denmark’s criminal code, which covers assisting a foreign intelligence service, as well as attempted murder. They denied wrongdoing in court, the broadcaster DR reported.

Kieffer-Kristensen said: “A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and risk-taking Russia.

“We believe that the case is important for understanding the threat that Denmark faces from Russia.”

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stood in full solidarity with Denmark and with all member states targeted by Russian hybrid attacks. She said the bloc would soon propose a “new European security strategy” to reinforce preparedness and deterrence.

The Russian embassy in Copenhagen said that Denmark’s accusations were not backed with proof.

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-21 14:03 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles

LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.

With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.

Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.

"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.

Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren't presented as evidence during the trial.

Juror says Rinderknecht's own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict

Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.

"It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said. "After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he's guilty."

Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a "lack of information" presented to the jury about the technical review.

In the end, it was Rinderknecht's own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.

"Stating that he was up on the hill, didn't smell a fire, didn't see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night," Cameron said.

Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been 'mad at everything'

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did.

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.

They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

"He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"

These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.

They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.

Defense argues fire's origin is unproven

Haney cast doubt on the government's case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.

The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.

Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors' request to strike his testimony.

Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.

He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act."…

Source: NPR News | Published: 2026-11-21 13:58 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.

He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".

Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."

In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".

The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.

It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

item.title: Riemann hypothesis: Has the world’s most famous maths problem been cracked?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Riemann hypothesis: Has the world’s most famous maths problem been cracked?

Mathematicians say the claimed proof, made with Claude, could be historic, but it may take weeks to understand it.

A mathematician from the tech giant Anthropic claims to have proven one of the world’s most famous – and most elusive – maths problems with the help of AI.

Levent Alpoge wrote on his website on Friday: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”

If his claim holds up, the proof he says he has would settle a question that has defeated mathematicians for 167 years. Independent experts are now trying to verify it, but so far no human has read through the entire argument.

Here is what we know.

What is the Riemann hypothesis?

First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is widely regarded as the most important open question in pure mathematics.

Prime numbers are whole numbers which can be divided only by one and themselves, such as 2, 3, 5 and 7. They appear to be scattered along the number line with no obvious pattern but the Riemann hypothesis proposes that their overall distribution actually follows a deep, hidden order – just one that humans have yet to identify.

“The Riemann hypothesis is the most famous and important unsolved problem in mathematics,” Abhishek Saha, professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.

“The patterns of the primes are encoded in a mathematical object called the Riemann zeta function, introduced by Bernhard Riemann in 1859.”

It is one of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1m award.

What has the Anthropic mathematician claimed?

Alpoge, a member of the company’s technical staff, made the announcement on Friday in a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said the proof he has found covers the generalised Riemann hypothesis, which extends the original conjecture to a broader family of mathematical functions.

He did not publish a conventional paper. Alpoge released the argument in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks reasoning step by step. He was open about how much of the work was Claude’s, writing that “Claude far outpaced me near the finish line”.

Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said nobody yet understands what the proof actually shows.

“At the minute, we don’t even know why the theorem is true,” he told Al Jazeera. “It’s 17 million lines of Lean code, and this might correspond to tens of thousands of pages of mathematics. We don’t even yet know how much of this mathematics is new ideas, how much of it is just sort of standard stuff the machine just had to develop.

“At the minute, the proof is just millions of lines of gobbledygook written in a strange programming language,” he said. “And right now, as we speak, there’s people all over the world who are translating parts of this programming language back into English.”

He expects answers to come fairly soon, however. “Experience shows you that you give the humans the Lean code, and within a week or two, they have a much better understanding of what’s actually going on in this code,” he said.

Why is the Riemann hypothesis so important?

“The implications of this hypothesis extend across large parts of mathematics, and hundreds of other mathematical results have been proved assuming this hypothesis is true,” Saha said. “A proof would settle a question that has occupied some of the greatest mathematical minds for over 160 years.”

Buzzard said the result also matters beyond pure mathematics, including for internet security.

“We know there are some algorithms that we run where they’re very quick, but we don’t actually know for sure if they work,” he said. “They seem to work, and we know that if the generalised Riemann hypothesis is true, then they do work.”

He said cryptographers had long worked on the assumption that the Riemann hypothesis is true. “In practice, people do tend to assume that the Riemann hypothesis is true because it’s a viable hypothesis to assume, because there’s so much evidence that it’s true,” he said. “But we can sleep slightly safer in our beds at night because it is true.”

Buzzard said the result stands out among recent AI breakthroughs in mathematics. He compared it with the Navier-Stokes problem, another Millennium Prize problem, which OpenAI said an unreleased AI model had solved in September. “That one doesn’t really have any applications at all,” he said, calling it “just of theoretical interest”. “Whereas the Riemann hypothesis has applications to neighbouring fields.

“It’s a very hard problem, but it’s definitely not the hardest problem in mathematics,” he said, pointing to even stronger versions such as the “extended Riemann hypothesis and the grand Riemann hypothesis”.

“The Riemann hypothesis is just, in some sense, at the foot of a mountain,” he said. “We’re beginning our trek up the mountain with this theorem.”

Why has it remained so elusive for so long?

“The problem is relatively simple to state, but extraordinarily difficult to prove,” Saha said. “Mathematicians have developed vast amounts of sophisticated theory in their attempts to solve it, but none of the techniques developed over the past 167 years has been sufficient. The direct methods have all been tried, and none of them come close to resolving it.

“Until very recently, most mathematicians, myself included, believed that a proof would require substantial new mathematical theories, perhaps developed over the next few decades.”

He said the claimed proof had overturned his expectations. “My own intuition was that we were still several years away from a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. This claimed proof, if correct, shatters my model of reality,” he said.…

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-21 12:49 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100
